strengths: The MoAA approach is a novel and promising direction for model alignment, effectively harnessing the diverse capabilities of open-source LLMs through a structured collaboration framework.
The paper demonstrates that the MoA-generated synthetic data leads to substantial performance gains in both SFT and DPO stages, highlighting the value of leveraging collective intelligence.
The performance on AlpacaEval and Arena-Hard is largely improved.
MoAA offers a good way to distill the abilities of stronger models into smaller ones.
The dataset could be useful to improve open-source models.
A simple and intuitive approach that leverages multiple open-source models for generating high-quality synthetic data for model alignment.
The approach demonstrates performance gains over baselines across datasets.
The paper provides a detailed analysis, offering insights into the impact of each training stage.
This paper is well-written and has easily understood figures.
The experimental improvement is quite significant.
The idea of using a mix of agents is intuitive and makes sense, as it is expected to improve data quality and reduce biases from a single model.
MoAA presents a competitive method to create high-quality instruction-following data only using open-source models.

The authors conducted many evaluations and ablation studies about MoAA. Empirical results show that training LMs with MoAA-curated data surpasses other methods such as directly using a single model (e.g., GPT-4o) to generate/judge responses.
weaknesses: This work can be summarized as directly applying MoA to create data, followed by standard SFT and DPO training, limiting its novelty and appearing incremental.

Many empirical choices in MoAA (e.g., model ensemble) affect performance and generalizability; the authors performed an empirical sweep to select models, making extension to other domains (math, coding, agentic tasks) highly impractical.

The presented results are potentially misleading because they compare MoAA-generated data against no-training or single-agent data, lacking a baseline of directly training on existing UltraChat and UltraFeedback data with SFT/DPO.
The compute‑cost‑performance trade‑off is not justified; the paper should compare inference cost of MoAA (using multiple 70B+ models) against proprietary models such as GPT‑4o.
The novelty is limited since MoA was previously proposed and not further optimized in this work.
No ablation study on the choice of mixed models.

Using the mixed‑model reward may degrade performance on certain tasks despite higher average scores driven by safety ratings; the number of safety tasks is low, raising questions about reward model choices.
MoAA’s effectiveness should be validated on more complex tasks (math, reasoning, coding) to assess generalizability.
Limited novelty: the paper primarily extends existing methodologies (MoA) with practical refinements rather than new techniques.
Weak baselines: only open‑source instruction‑tuned models are compared, lacking stronger baselines such as [1,2].
Limited model evaluation: only Llama 3.1 8B and Gemma 2 9B are evaluated; broader range of model sizes/architectures would better assess generalizability.
Technical contributions are relatively limited; the pipeline largely relies on existing work (MoA) to construct preference data for SFT and DPO.
The only technical differences are adjusting prompts, making multi‑turn data compatible, and adding a dynamic criteria filtering component, which yields minimal improvement (~one point).

Comparisons with related works are insufficient; mainly compare MoAA to base model or other MoAA settings, lacking broader comparisons (e.g., to MoA, other reward models) and MoAA sometimes fails to outperform alternative models.
Experiments are limited to small 8/9B models; scalability to larger models is uncertain.
Dataset construction incurs higher costs; lack of analysis on construction efficiency (e.g., number of LLM calls or tokens consumed) limits perspective.

The strong models used as proposers/aggregators (WizardLM-8x22B, Qwen1.5-110B-Chat) are stronger than the target models; it would be more compelling if the trained model could surpass those source models, but such comparison is missing.
